**﴿For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their accustomed journeys in winter and summer, so let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.﴾**

This is a novel opening, since it begins with a prepositional phrase governed by the preposition *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), and there is nothing close by in the sentence that could be linked to it. This creates suspense about what the prepositional phrase depends on. The suspense is heightened by the length of the sentence, since the phrase is separated from what it governs by five words. Thus *li-ilaf* (for the accustomed security) is connected to the words *fal-ya'budu* (so let them worship).

Placing this prepositional phrase first serves to emphasize it, for it is among the reasons for commanding them to worship God, a worship they had abandoned in favour of idol-worship. The prepositional phrase is connected to the verb *li-ya'budu* (let them worship).

The original arrangement of the sentence would be: "Let Quraysh worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear, for the security of their journeys in winter and summer." When the intended emphasis required placing the object before its governing verb, the fronting produced a meaning that made the phrase a condition for its verb. Therefore the verb was joined with the *fa'* (so), which normally belongs to the apodosis of a conditional sentence. The *fa'* that enters the words *fal-ya'budu* indicates that what precedes it has the force of a condition. In other words, it indicates that the fronting of the object is intended to express special emphasis and strong concern, the concern of one who sets a condition for something, while the rest of the sentence is suspended upon it, awaiting its answer. This is a concise and original style.

In *al-Kashshaf*, it is said: "The *fa'* entered because of the sense of condition in the sentence, for the meaning is: either not [worship Him], so let them worship Him for their security, that is, the blessings of God upon them are beyond counting. If they do not worship Him for all His blessings, then let them worship Him for this single blessing, which is a manifest blessing." End of quotation.

Al-Zajjaj said, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord, so magnify﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:3], "The *fa'* entered to convey the sense of condition, as if it were said: 'Whatever [may be], do not abandon His magnification.'" End of quotation. This is the same meaning as in *al-Kashshaf*. Both of them remained silent about the source from which the sense of condition arises, and that is because such a construction applies when a prepositional phrase or similar complement of the verb is fronted. Consider the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Me, fear [only] Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:40] in the Sura of al-Baqarah; and among such constructions is His saying: ﴿So let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus 10:58] in the Sura of Yunus; and His saying: ﴿So for that, call [them], and remain steadfast﴾ [al-Shura 42:15] in the Sura of al-Shura. And there is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the man who asked him about jihad: he said to him, "Do you have parents?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then strive in service to them."

It is also permissible to make the *lam* dependent on a verb of wonder (*i'jabu*), omitted, which the *lam* indicates, because the *lam* is very frequently used with a complement after expressions of wonder. One says: "How strange, for you!" and "How strange, for that matter!" Among such uses is the line of Imru' al-Qays: "*fa-ya laka min layl*" ("Oh, what a night it is!"). Since the vocative particle is meant here to express wonder, the *fa'* in the words *fal-ya'budu* will be a consequence of the wonder.

Al-Farra' and Ibn Ishaq in *al-Sira* permitted that ﴿for the security of Quraysh﴾ be connected to what is in the Sura of al-Fil, namely His saying: ﴿and He made them like eaten straw﴾ [al-Fil 105:5]. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid and the narration of Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is like *tadmin* (interlocking) in poetry, which is that the meaning of a verse is connected to the one before it in a way that is valid only through it." End of quotation. They mean that although this Sura is an independent Sura, it is attached to the Sura of al-Fil. Just as a verse is attached to a verse revealed before it, so too are passages that form a Sura attached to, and dependent upon, a Sura revealed before it.

*Al-ilaf* is the verbal noun of *a'lafa*, with two hamzas, meaning *alifa* (to be accustomed), and both are dialectal forms. The original is *alifa*, and the *if'al* form in it is for intensification, because its original function is to indicate that an action occurs from both sides. It came to be used to convey the verbal sense of the act metaphorically, and then this usage spread to some verbs until it equaled the literal sense, as in *safara* (to travel), *'afahu Allah* (God granted him well-being), and *qatalahumu Allah* (God fought them).

Most readers recite it in both places as *li-ilaf* with a *ya'* after the hamza, which is a softening of the second hamza. Ibn 'Amir recited the first *li-ilaf* as *li-ilaf* (without the *ya'*), which is the one whose original is a second hamza, and he recited *ilafihim* with the *ya'* like the majority. Abu Ja'far recited *li-ilaf Quraysh* with the first hamza omitted, and he recited *ilafihim* with a kasra-marked hamza and without a *ya'*.

Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi mentioned that Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, recited with the two hamzas made clear in *li-i'laf* and *i'lafihim*. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned on the authority of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that the clarifying of the two hamzas has no valid basis. I say: no book of readings known to us attributes this reading to Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim. What is well known is that 'Asim agrees with the majority in making the second of the two hamzas a *ya'*, so this is a weak narration from Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim.

The word was written in the Qur'anic codex (*al-Mushaf*) as *ilafihim* without a *ya'* after the hamza. As for the lengthening *alif* that comes after the *lam*, which is the root letter of the word, it was not written in the two words in the codex, according to the habit with most such lengthening vowels. The readings are transmitted narrations, and the orthography of the codex is nothing but a reminder to the reader. The writing of the codex is a followed tradition established by the Companions who were appointed to copy the codices.

The construction of *ilaf* with Quraysh is a genitive construction in the sense of the verbal noun with its agent, with its object omitted, because here it is used in the nominal sense of that custom. So it is a semantic genitive construction, with the *lam* understood.

*Quraysh* is the title of the forefather who gathers many clans. He is Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinana. This is the view of the majority of genealogists, and everyone above Fihr is from Kinana. Fihr was given the title Quraysh in the diminutive form. According to the correct view, it is the diminutive of *qarsh*, with a fatha on the qaf, a sukun on the ra', and a shin with a dot. It is the name of a kind of fish, strong, which attacks fish and ships.

Some genealogists said that Quraysh is the title of al-Nadr ibn Kinana. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he was asked about Quraysh, and he said: "They are from the descendants of al-Nadr." In another narration he said: "We are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana; we do not deny our mother, nor do we disown our father." So all the people of Mecca are Quraysh, and among them were distributed the offices of the people of Mecca in the pre-Islamic period. The clans of Kinana were in Khayf Mina, and they had offices specifically concerning the affairs of the pilgrimage, among which was the *nasi'* (the intercalation of months).

His saying *ilafihim* is an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) of *ilaf Quraysh*, and it is from the style of summarization (*ijmal*). The detailing is for the sake of giving attention to the news, so that it settles in the mind of the listener. Among such uses is the saying of the Exalted, quoting Pharaoh: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, the means to the heavens﴾ [Ghafir 40:36], and the line of Imru' al-Qays: "And on the day I entered the litter, the litter of 'Unayza."

*Al-rihla*, with a kasra on the ra', is a noun for departure, which is travel from one place to another far away. For this reason, the camel on which one travels is called *rahila*.

The genitive construction *rihla* with *al-shita'* (winter) is from the construction of an action to its time in which it occurs. Sometimes the action fills its time, like the expression *sahar al-layl* (the night's vigil). Sometimes it is only the time of its beginning, like the *salat al-zuhr* (the noon prayer). The apparent sense of the construction is that the journeys of winter and summer are known and familiar, and they are two journeys. So "and summer" is coordinated with an elided noun, that is, "and the journey of summer," because it is evident that one journey cannot begin in two seasons. It is therefore established that they are two journeys in two periods.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the singular word *rihla* be in the genitive construction with two things, since the meaning is clear and there is no ambiguity. Abu Hayyan said: according to Sibawayh, this is not permitted except in cases of necessity.

*Al-shita'* is the name of a season of the solar year, which is divided into four seasons. The season of winter is eighty-nine days and some minutes, beginning with the sun's entry into the sign of Capricorn (*al-Jady*), and ending with the sun's exit from the sign of Pisces (*al-Hut*). Its signs are three: Capricorn, Aquarius (*al-Dalw*), and Pisces. The season of winter is the period of cold.

*Al-sayf* is the name of a season of the solar year, and it is the time of heat. Its duration is ninety-three days and some hours, beginning with the sun's entry into the sign of Cancer (*al-Saratan*), and ending with the sun's exit from the sign of Virgo (*al-Sunbula*). Its signs are three: Cancer, Leo (*al-Asad*), and Virgo.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik said, "Winter is half the year, and summer is half of it. I have always seen Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman and those with him not removing their turbans until the Pleiades (*al-Thurayya*) rises." (He means the rising of the Pleiades at dawn, and that is the first part of summer.) This is the nineteenth day of Bashans, which is the twenty-fifth day according to the Roman or Persian reckoning. End of quotation. The month of Bashans is the ninth of the months of the Coptic year, which is divided into twelve months.

The month of Bashans begins on the twenty-sixth day of the month of Nisan (April), and it is thirty days, ending on the 25th of the month of Iyar (May).

The rising of the Pleiades at dawn is on the nineteenth day of the month of Bashans among the months of the Copts. The linguists said: summer, according to common usage, is half the year, which is six months, and winter is half the year, which is six months.

Strictly speaking, the year has four seasons: summer is three months, which is what the people of Iraq and Khurasan call spring (*al-rabi'*). Next comes *al-qayz*, three months, which is the intensity of heat. Next comes *al-kharif* (autumn), three months. Next comes winter, three months. This verse is suitable for both terminologies. The terminology of the scholars of the calendar (*al-miqat*) is to divide the year into spring (*rabi'*), summer, autumn (*kharif*), and winter, and the beginning of the year is spring, which is the sun's entry into the sign of Aries (*al-Hamal*).

These two journeys were journeys of trade and provisioning, which Quraysh prepared in these two seasons of the year: one in winter, to the land of Abyssinia, then to Yemen, reaching with them the land of Himyar; and the other in summer, to Syria, reaching with them the city of Busra in the land of Syria.

The one who established these two journeys for them was Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf. The reason for this was that they were afflicted by destitution. When a household did not have food for its sustenance, the head of the household would carry his dependents to a known place, pitch a tent over them, and they would remain there until they died of hunger. This was called *al-i'tifar* (with an unpointed 'ayn, and with a ra', and it was said with a dal instead of the ra', and with a fa'). It happened that a household from the clan of Banu Makhzum was struck by severe poverty, and they resolved to practice *al-i'tifar*. The news reached Hashim, because one of their sons was a foster-brother (*tirb*) of Asad ibn Hashim. Hashim stood up as a speaker among Quraysh and said: "You have introduced an innovation by which you become few and the Arabs multiply, you become humiliated and the Arabs are honoured. You are the people of the sanctuary of God, and the people are followers of you. And this *i'tifar* is about to come upon you." Then he gathered all the sons of one father into two journeys for trade. Whatever the wealthy man gained, he divided between himself and the poor of his clan, until their poor became like their rich. Concerning this, Matrud al-Khuza'i said:

"O man who changes his saddle-bag,
Would that you had alighted with the family of 'Abd Manaf!
Those who take the covenant from its horizons,
And those who journey for the journey of *al-ilaf*.
And those who mix their rich with their poor,
Until their poor becomes like the sufficient."

The two journeys of the *ilaf* of Quraysh continued until Islam came, and they were still upon that.

The well-known and widely reported view is that the one who instituted the *ilaf* (the covenant of safe passage) was Hashim. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-'Arabi reports from al-Harawi that the holders of the *ilaf* were Hashim and his three brothers: 'Abd Shams, al-Muttalib, and Nawfal. Each of them took a *habl* (a covenant, i.e. a pledge of protection) from one of the kings through whose lands they traded: the King of Syria, the King of Abyssinia, the King of Yemen, and the King of Persia. Hashim took it from the King of Syria, who was the King of the Romans. 'Abd Shams took it from the Negus of Abyssinia, al-Muttalib took it from the King of Yemen, and Nawfal took it from Kisra, King of Persia. They would give a *ju'l* (a fee) to the chiefs of the tribes and the leaders of the clans, which was also called *ilaf*. They gave them a share of the profit, carried goods for them, and drove camels to them alongside their own camels, so as to spare them the burden of travel. In return, they protected Quraysh from enemies. Through this, they secured the whole route to Yemen and to Syria, and they were called *al-mujirun* (the protectors).

Al-Naqqash imagined from this that each of these four had a separate journey, and so he claimed that there were four *rihal* (caravan journeys). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view is rejected." Ibn 'Atiyya is right, for the fact that the parties to the covenant by which the *ilaf* was made were four does not require that the journeys be four, since no one has said that. Perhaps these brothers took turns in accompanying the journeys, because they were well known to the tribes through whose lands the caravan passed. Or perhaps they inherited this role after Hashim's death, so that the caravan was attributed to one of them, just as they attributed the caravan that the Muslims intercepted at Badr to Abu Sufyan, since he was then the leader of the people of the valley in Makkah.

The meaning of the verse is a reminder to Quraysh of God's favour upon them: He made easy for them what was not possible for other Arabs, namely security from the aggression of attackers and the raids of raiders throughout the whole year. He also made easy for them the building of the Ka'bah, the institution of the Hajj, their being the custodians of the Sacred Mosque, and He gave them dignity and reverence in the hearts of all the Arabs, both during the sacred months and at other times.

Among the tribes that did not observe the sacred months, such as Tayyi', Quda'ah, and Khath'am, [the journeys] were also made easy for Quraysh, so that the Arab lands from south to north became accessible to them. People in need took refuge with them and travelled with them, and merchants loaded their wares onto them. Makkah became a central point to which goods were brought from all the Arab lands, and from there they were distributed to those who sought them in the rest of the country. Thus the people of Makkah became rich through trade, since they were not people of cultivation or of herding, for they lived in a valley without cultivation. They used to import their food: from Yemen they brought grains of wheat, barley, sorghum, and raisins, as well as leather, cloth, and Yemeni swords; and from Syria they brought grains, dates, olive oil, raisins, cloth, and the *mashrafiyyah* swords. This was in addition to the sacred months that were granted to them along with most of the Arabs, and the festivals and markets of the Hajj that were established for them, as indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾.

This is the explanation for why the command to worship is tied specifically to the favour of this *ilaf*, although God has many favours upon them. This is because the *ilaf* was a comprehensive cause for the most important of the blessings on which their continued existence depended.

The discussion of the meaning of the *fa'* in His words ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ has already been dealt with above, in all its aspects.

The worship they were commanded to perform is the worship of God alone, without associating partners with Him in worship. This is because associating with God someone who does not deserve worship, alongside Him who alone deserves it, is not worship at all. Alternatively, they were preoccupied with worshipping idols instead of God, so they did not mention God except during the days of the Hajj, in the *talbiyah* (the call of pilgrimage). Even so, some of them added to it, after their saying "Labbayka, la sharika laka" (Here I am, You have no partner), the words "illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malaka" (except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns).

The expression of the Lord ("Rabb") as an annexed noun to ﴿this House﴾, rather than saying "So let them worship God," is because the word "Rabb" implies that He deserves to be worshipped exclusively, without any partner.

The annexation of "Rabb" to ﴿this House﴾ was preferred over saying "Their Lord," in order to allude to the fact that the House is the origin of the favour of the *ilaf*, since He commanded Abraham to build the Sacred House, and it was thus the cause of their elevated status among the Arabs. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for mankind﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 97]. This is an incidental reference (*idmaj*) that honours the Sacred House and its excellence.

The House is already known to those addressed, so it is pointed to, because by that prior familiarity it was as though present in the context of the speech. Moreover, the House, defined in this way with the definite article, became a proper name by dominance over the Ka'bah, and the Lord of the House is God, a fact the Arabs acknowledge.

The description of the Lord is given in the relative form ﴿Who fed them against hunger﴾, because of what it implies as a reason for the command to worship the Lord of the Sacred House, by another cause in addition to the favour of making trade easy for them. This is what made them people of wealth, and these two are the favours of feeding them and securing them. This refers to the way in which the ships of Abyssinia were made to come by sea to Jeddah, carrying food to sell there. Quraysh used to go out to Jeddah with camels and donkeys and buy food, a journey of two nights. The people of Taba'lah and Jurash, in the fertile lands of Yemen, used to bring food to Makkah, so they lived in abundance because of the plentiful food in their own land. Likewise, markets were made to be held around Makkah during the months of the Hajj: the market of Majannah, the market of Dhu al-Majaz, and the market of 'Ukaz. There, provisions came to them and their livelihood became broad. It also refers to the fear of Makkah and its people that God placed in the hearts of the Arabs, so that no one wished to harm them by intimidation. This is the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure town and provide its people with fruits﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 126]. This [provision] did not cease to reach them except when the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated against them with the words: "O God, make [the famine] upon them as the years of Joseph." Then they were struck by famine and drought for seven years, and that was at the beginning of the Hijrah.

The *min* that is attached to *ju'* (hunger) and to *khawf* (fear) has the meaning of substitution (*badaliyyah*), that is: He fed them in place of hunger, and secured them in place of fear. The meaning of substitution is that the condition of their land required that its people be hungry. Thus feeding them is a substitute for the hunger that their land would necessitate. Likewise, their condition of small numbers, their being settled people and not people of war, valour, or armed strength, would require that they be exposed to the raids of the tribes. So God gave them security in the Sanctuary instead of the fear that their paucity would entail. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 67].

The indefiniteness of *ju'* (hunger) and *khawf* (fear) is for specification of kind, not for magnification, since no great hunger or fear had befallen them before. Musawwar ibn Hind said in satire of the Banu Asad:

You claimed that your brothers are Quraysh,
for them is the *ilaf*, and for you there is no *ilaf*.
Those were made secure against hunger and fear,
while the Banu Asad have hungered and feared.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Ma'un

This surah is called "Surat al-Ma'un" in many mushafs (codices of the Qur'an) and books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), because the word *al-ma'un* occurs in it and in no other surah.

In some tafsir works it is called "Surat Ara'ayta" (Surat Have You Seen), and likewise in a mushaf from al-Qayrawan from the fifth century; and also al-Bukhari entitled it so in his Sahih.

Ibn 'Atiyya titled it "Surat Ara'ayta alladhi" (Surat Have You Seen the One Who). Al-Kawashi, in *al-Talkhis*, called it "Surat al-Ma'un, al-Din, and Ara'ayta." In *al-Itqan*, it is said: "It is also called Surat al-Din (The Surah of Religion)." In the marginal notes of al-Khafaji and Sa'di it is called Surat al-Takdhib (The Surah of Denial). Al-Biqa'i in *Nazm al-Durar* called it Surat al-Yatim (The Surah of the Orphan). These are six names.

It is Meccan according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Qurtubi reported from Qatadah that it is Medinan, and this is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. In *al-Itqan* it is said: it is said that three verses were revealed first in Makkah, namely up to His words "the poor" (*al-miskin*), and the rest was revealed in Madinah. That is, on the basis that His words ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [Al-Ma'un: 4] through the end of the surah refer to the hypocrites. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Hibat Allah al-Darir, and it is the most apparent view.

It is counted as the seventeenth in the order of the revelation of the surahs, on the basis that it is Meccan. It was revealed after Surat al-Takathur and before Surat al-Kafirun.

Its verses are counted as six by the majority of counters. Al-Alusi related that those who counted its verses as six were the people of Iraq (i.e., Basra and Kufa). Al-Shaykh 'Ali al-Nuri al-Safaqsi said in *Ghayth al-Naf'*: "Its verses are seven according to the Himsi (i.e., Syrian) count, and six in the rest." This contradicts what al-Alusi said.

Among the purposes of this surah is to express astonishment at the state of those who denied the Resurrection, and to condemn their actions: their aggression against the weak and their contempt for him, their withholding of food from the poor, and their turning away from the foundations of Islam, such as prayer and zakat. This is because it does not occur to them that their conduct may bring upon them the anger and punishment of God.

It came to be used to convey the verbal sense of the act metaphorically, and then this usage spread to some verbs until it equaled the literal sense, as in *safara* (to travel), *'afahu Allah* (God granted him well-being), and *qatalahumu Allah* (God fought them).

Most readers recite it in both places as *li-ilaf* with a *ya'* after the hamza, which is a softening of the second hamza. Ibn 'Amir recited the first *li-ilaf* as *li-ilaf* (without the *ya'*), which is the one whose original is a second hamza, and he recited *ilafihim* with the *ya'* like the majority. Abu Ja'far recited *li-ilaf Quraysh* with the first hamza omitted, and he recited *ilafihim* with a kasra-marked hamza and without a *ya'*.

Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi mentioned that Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, recited with the two hamzas made clear in *li-i'laf* and *i'lafihim*. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned on the authority of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that the clarifying of the two hamzas has no valid basis. I say: no book of readings known to us attributes this reading to Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim. What is well known is that 'Asim agrees with the majority in making the second of the two hamzas a *ya'*, so this is a weak narration from Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim.

The word was written in the Qur'anic codex (*al-Mushaf*) as *ilafihim* without a *ya'* after the hamza. As for the lengthening *alif* that comes after the *lam*, which is the root letter of the word, it was not written in the two words in the codex, according to the habit with most such lengthening vowels. The readings are transmitted narrations, and the orthography of the codex is nothing but a reminder to the reader. The writing of the codex is a followed tradition established by the Companions who were appointed to copy the codices.

The construction of *ilaf* with Quraysh is a genitive construction in the sense of the verbal noun with its agent, with its object omitted, because here it is used in the nominal sense of that custom. So it is a semantic genitive construction, with the *lam* understood.

*Quraysh* is the title of the forefather who gathers many clans. He is Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinana. This is the view of the majority of genealogists, and everyone above Fihr is from Kinana. Fihr was given the title Quraysh in the diminutive form. According to the correct view, it is the diminutive of *qarsh*, with a fatha on the qaf, a sukun on the ra', and a shin with a dot. It is the name of a kind of fish, strong, which attacks fish and ships.

Some genealogists said that Quraysh is the title of al-Nadr ibn Kinana. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he was asked about Quraysh, and he said: "They are from the descendants of al-Nadr." In another narration he said: "We are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana; we do not deny our mother, nor do we disown our father." So all the people of Mecca are Quraysh, and among them were distributed the offices of the people of Mecca in the pre-Islamic period. The clans of Kinana were in Khayf Mina, and they had offices specifically concerning the affairs of the pilgrimage, among which was the *nasi'* (the intercalation of months).

His saying *ilafihim* is an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) of *ilaf Quraysh*, and it is from the style of summarization (*ijmal*). The detailing is for the sake of giving attention to the news, so that it settles in the mind of the listener. Among such uses is the saying of the Exalted, quoting Pharaoh: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, the means to the heavens﴾ [Ghafir 40:36], and the line of Imru' al-Qays: "And on the day I entered the litter, the litter of 'Unayza."

*Al-rihla*, with a kasra on the ra', is a noun for departure, which is travel from one place to another far away. For this reason, the camel on which one travels is called *rahila*.

The genitive construction *rihla* with *al-shita'* (winter) is from the construction of an action to its time in which it occurs. Sometimes the action fills its time, like the expression *sahar al-layl* (the night's vigil). Sometimes it is only the time of its beginning, like the *salat al-zuhr* (the noon prayer). The apparent sense of the construction is that the journeys of winter and summer are known and familiar, and they are two journeys. So "and summer" is coordinated with an elided noun, that is, "and the journey of summer," because it is evident that one journey cannot begin in two seasons. It is therefore established that they are two journeys in two periods.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the singular word *rihla* be in the genitive construction with two things, since the meaning is clear and there is no ambiguity. Abu Hayyan said: according to Sibawayh, this is not permitted except in cases of necessity.

*Al-shita'* is the name of a season of the solar year, which is divided into four seasons. The season of winter is eighty-nine days and some minutes, beginning with the sun's entry into the sign of Capricorn (*al-Jady*), and ending with the sun's exit from the sign of Pisces (*al-Hut*). Its signs are three: Capricorn, Aquarius (*al-Dalw*), and Pisces. The season of winter is the period of cold.

*Al-sayf* is the name of a season of the solar year, and it is the time of heat. Its duration is ninety-three days and some hours, beginning with the sun's entry into the sign of Cancer (*al-Saratan*), and ending with the sun's exit from the sign of Virgo (*al-Sunbula*). Its signs are three: Cancer, Leo (*al-Asad*), and Virgo.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik said, "Winter is half the year, and summer is half of it. I have always seen Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman and those with him not removing their turbans until the Pleiades (*al-Thurayya*) rises." (He means the rising of the Pleiades at dawn, and that is the first part of summer.) This is the nineteenth day of Bashans, which is the twenty-fifth day according to the Roman or Persian reckoning. End of quotation. The month of Bashans is the ninth of the months of the Coptic year, which is divided into twelve months.

The month of Bashans begins on the twenty-sixth day of the month of Nisan (April), and it is thirty days, ending on the 25th of the month of Iyar (May).

The rising of the Pleiades at dawn is on the nineteenth day of the month of Bashans among the months of the Copts. The linguists said: summer, according to common usage, is half the year, which is six months, and winter is half the year, which is six months.

Strictly speaking, the year has four seasons: summer is three months, which is what the people of Iraq and Khurasan call spring (*al-rabi'*). Next comes *al-qayz*, three months, which is the intensity of heat. Next comes *al-kharif* (autumn), three months. Next comes winter, three months. This verse is suitable for both terminologies. The terminology of the scholars of the calendar (*al-miqat*) is to divide the year into spring (*rabi'*), summer, autumn (*kharif*), and winter, and the beginning of the year is spring, which is the sun's entry into the sign of Aries (*al-Hamal*).

These two journeys were journeys of trade and provisioning, which Quraysh prepared in these two seasons of the year: one in winter, to the land of Abyssinia, then to Yemen, reaching with them the land of Himyar; and the other in summer, to Syria, reaching with them the city of Busra in the land of Syria.

The one who established these two journeys for them was Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf. The reason for this was that they were afflicted by destitution. When a household did not have food for its sustenance, the head of the household would carry his dependents to a known place, pitch a tent over them, and they would remain there until they died of hunger. This was called *al-i'tifar* (with an unpointed 'ayn, and with a ra', and it was said with a dal instead of the ra', and with a fa'). It happened that a household from the clan of Banu Makhzum was struck by severe poverty, and they resolved to practice *al-i'tifar*. The news reached Hashim, because one of their sons was a foster-brother (*tirb*) of Asad ibn Hashim. Hashim stood up as a speaker among Quraysh and said: "You have introduced an innovation by which you become few and the Arabs multiply, you become humiliated and the Arabs are honoured. You are the people of the sanctuary of God, and the people are followers of you. And this *i'tifar* is about to come upon you." Then he gathered all the sons of one father into two journeys for trade. Whatever the wealthy man gained, he divided between himself and the poor of his clan, until their poor became like their rich. Concerning this, Matrud al-Khuza'i said:

"O man who changes his saddle-bag,
Would that you had alighted with the family of 'Abd Manaf!
Those who take the covenant from its horizons,
And those who journey for the journey of *al-ilaf*.
And those who mix their rich with their poor,
Until their poor becomes like the sufficient."

The two journeys of the *ilaf* of Quraysh continued until Islam came, and they were still upon that.

The well-known and widely reported view is that the one who instituted the *ilaf* (the covenant of safe passage) was Hashim. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-'Arabi reports from al-Harawi that the holders of the *ilaf* were Hashim and his three brothers: 'Abd Shams, al-Muttalib, and Nawfal. Each of them took a *habl* (a covenant, i.e. a pledge of protection) from one of the kings through whose lands they traded: the King of Syria, the King of Abyssinia, the King of Yemen, and the King of Persia. Hashim took it from the King of Syria, who was the King of the Romans. 'Abd Shams took it from the Negus of Abyssinia, al-Muttalib took it from the King of Yemen, and Nawfal took it from Kisra, King of Persia. They would give a *ju'l* (a fee) to the chiefs of the tribes and the leaders of the clans, which was also called *ilaf*. They gave them a share of the profit, carried goods for them, and drove camels to them alongside their own camels, so as to spare them the burden of travel. In return, they protected Quraysh from enemies. Through this, they secured the whole route to Yemen and to Syria, and they were called *al-mujirun* (the protectors).

Al-Naqqash imagined from this that each of these four had a separate journey, and so he claimed that there were four *rihal* (caravan journeys). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view is rejected." Ibn 'Atiyya is right, for the fact that the parties to the covenant by which the *ilaf* was made were four does not require that the journeys be four, since no one has said that. Perhaps these brothers took turns in accompanying the journeys, because they were well known to the tribes through whose lands the caravan passed. Or perhaps they inherited this role after Hashim's death, so that the caravan was attributed to one of them, just as they attributed the caravan that the Muslims intercepted at Badr to Abu Sufyan, since he was then the leader of the people of the valley in Makkah.

The meaning of the verse is a reminder to Quraysh of God's favour upon them: He made easy for them what was not possible for other Arabs, namely security from the aggression of attackers and the raids of raiders throughout the whole year. He also made easy for them the building of the Ka'bah, the institution of the Hajj, their being the custodians of the Sacred Mosque, and He gave them dignity and reverence in the hearts of all the Arabs, both during the sacred months and at other times.

Among the tribes that did not observe the sacred months, such as Tayyi', Quda'ah, and Khath'am, [the journeys] were also made easy for Quraysh, so that the Arab lands from south to north became accessible to them. People in need took refuge with them and travelled with them, and merchants loaded their wares onto them. Makkah became a central point to which goods were brought from all the Arab lands, and from there they were distributed to those who sought them in the rest of the country. Thus the people of Makkah became rich through trade, since they were not people of cultivation or of herding, for they lived in a valley without cultivation. They used to import their food: from Yemen they brought grains of wheat, barley, sorghum, and raisins, as well as leather, cloth, and Yemeni swords; and from Syria they brought grains, dates, olive oil, raisins, cloth, and the *mashrafiyyah* swords. This was in addition to the sacred months that were granted to them along with most of the Arabs, and the festivals and markets of the Hajj that were established for them, as indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾.

This is the explanation for why the command to worship is tied specifically to the favour of this *ilaf*, although God has many favours upon them. This is because the *ilaf* was a comprehensive cause for the most important of the blessings on which their continued existence depended.

The discussion of the meaning of the *fa'* in His words ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ has already been dealt with above, in all its aspects.

The worship they were commanded to perform is the worship of God alone, without associating partners with Him in worship. This is because associating with God someone who does not deserve worship, alongside Him who alone deserves it, is not worship at all. Alternatively, they were preoccupied with worshipping idols instead of God, so they did not mention God except during the days of the Hajj, in the *talbiyah* (the call of pilgrimage). Even so, some of them added to it, after their saying "Labbayka, la sharika laka" (Here I am, You have no partner), the words "illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malaka" (except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns).

The expression of the Lord ("Rabb") as an annexed noun to ﴿this House﴾, rather than saying "So let them worship God," is because the word "Rabb" implies that He deserves to be worshipped exclusively, without any partner.

The annexation of "Rabb" to ﴿this House﴾ was preferred over saying "Their Lord," in order to allude to the fact that the House is the origin of the favour of the *ilaf*, since He commanded Abraham to build the Sacred House, and it was thus the cause of their elevated status among the Arabs. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for mankind﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 97]. This is an incidental reference (*idmaj*) that honours the Sacred House and its excellence.

The House is already known to those addressed, so it is pointed to, because by that prior familiarity it was as though present in the context of the speech. Moreover, the House, defined in this way with the definite article, became a proper name by dominance over the Ka'bah, and the Lord of the House is God, a fact the Arabs acknowledge.

The description of the Lord is given in the relative form ﴿Who fed them against hunger﴾, because of what it implies as a reason for the command to worship the Lord of the Sacred House, by another cause in addition to the favour of making trade easy for them. This is what made them people of wealth, and these two are the favours of feeding them and securing them. This refers to the way in which the ships of Abyssinia were made to come by sea to Jeddah, carrying food to sell there. Quraysh used to go out to Jeddah with camels and donkeys and buy food, a journey of two nights. The people of Taba'lah and Jurash, in the fertile lands of Yemen, used to bring food to Makkah, so they lived in abundance because of the plentiful food in their own land. Likewise, markets were made to be held around Makkah during the months of the Hajj: the market of Majannah, the market of Dhu al-Majaz, and the market of 'Ukaz. There, provisions came to them and their livelihood became broad. It also refers to the fear of Makkah and its people that God placed in the hearts of the Arabs, so that no one wished to harm them by intimidation. This is the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure town and provide its people with fruits﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 126]. This [provision] did not cease to reach them except when the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated against them with the words: "O God, make [the famine] upon them as the years of Joseph." Then they were struck by famine and drought for seven years, and that was at the beginning of the Hijrah.

The *min* that is attached to *ju'* (hunger) and to *khawf* (fear) has the meaning of substitution (*badaliyyah*), that is: He fed them in place of hunger, and secured them in place of fear. The meaning of substitution is that the condition of their land required that its people be hungry. Thus feeding them is a substitute for the hunger that their land would necessitate. Likewise, their condition of small numbers, their being settled people and not people of war, valour, or armed strength, would require that they be exposed to the raids of the tribes. So God gave them security in the Sanctuary instead of the fear that their paucity would entail. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 67].

The indefiniteness of *ju'* (hunger) and *khawf* (fear) is for specification of kind, not for magnification, since no great hunger or fear had befallen them before. Musawwar ibn Hind said in satire of the Banu Asad:

You claimed that your brothers are Quraysh,
for them is the *ilaf*, and for you there is no *ilaf*.
Those were made secure against hunger and fear,
while the Banu Asad have hungered and feared.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Ma'un

This surah is called "Surat al-Ma'un" in many mushafs (codices of the Qur'an) and books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), because the word *al-ma'un* occurs in it and in no other surah.

In some tafsir works it is called "Surat Ara'ayta" (Surat Have You Seen), and likewise in a mushaf from al-Qayrawan from the fifth century; and also al-Bukhari entitled it so in his Sahih.

Ibn 'Atiyya titled it "Surat Ara'ayta alladhi" (Surat Have You Seen the One Who). Al-Kawashi, in *al-Talkhis*, called it "Surat al-Ma'un, al-Din, and Ara'ayta." In *al-Itqan*, it is said: "It is also called Surat al-Din (The Surah of Religion)." In the marginal notes of al-Khafaji and Sa'di it is called Surat al-Takdhib (The Surah of Denial). Al-Biqa'i in *Nazm al-Durar* called it Surat al-Yatim (The Surah of the Orphan). These are six names.

It is Meccan according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Qurtubi reported from Qatadah that it is Medinan, and this is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. In *al-Itqan* it is said: it is said that three verses were revealed first in Makkah, namely up to His words "the poor" (*al-miskin*), and the rest was revealed in Madinah. That is, on the basis that His words ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [Al-Ma'un: 4] through the end of the surah refer to the hypocrites. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Hibat Allah al-Darir, and it is the most apparent view.

It is counted as the seventeenth in the order of the revelation of the surahs, on the basis that it is Meccan. It was revealed after Surat al-Takathur and before Surat al-Kafirun.

Its verses are counted as six by the majority of counters. Al-Alusi related that those who counted its verses as six were the people of Iraq (i.e., Basra and Kufa). Al-Shaykh 'Ali al-Nuri al-Safaqsi said in *Ghayth al-Naf'*: "Its verses are seven according to the Himsi (i.e., Syrian) count, and six in the rest." This contradicts what al-Alusi said.

Among the purposes of this surah is to express astonishment at the state of those who denied the Resurrection, and to condemn their actions: their aggression against the weak and their contempt for him, their withholding of food from the poor, and their turning away from the foundations of Islam, such as prayer and zakat. This is because it does not occur to them that their conduct may bring upon them the anger and punishment of God.

**﴿For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their accustomed journeys in winter and summer, so let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.﴾**

This is a novel opening, since it begins with a prepositional phrase governed by the preposition *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), and there is nothing close by in the sentence that could be linked to it. This creates suspense about what the prepositional phrase depends on. The suspense is heightened by the length of the sentence, since the phrase is separated from what it governs by five words. Thus *li-ilaf* (for the accustomed security) is connected to the words *fal-ya'budu* (so let them worship).

Placing this prepositional phrase first serves to emphasize it, for it is among the reasons for commanding them to worship God, a worship they had abandoned in favour of idol-worship. The prepositional phrase is connected to the verb *li-ya'budu* (let them worship).

The original arrangement of the sentence would be: "Let Quraysh worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear, for the security of their journeys in winter and summer." When the intended emphasis required placing the object before its governing verb, the fronting produced a meaning that made the phrase a condition for its verb. Therefore the verb was joined with the *fa'* (so), which normally belongs to the apodosis of a conditional sentence. The *fa'* that enters the words *fal-ya'budu* indicates that what precedes it has the force of a condition. In other words, it indicates that the fronting of the object is intended to express special emphasis and strong concern, the concern of one who sets a condition for something, while the rest of the sentence is suspended upon it, awaiting its answer. This is a concise and original style.

In *al-Kashshaf*, it is said: "The *fa'* entered because of the sense of condition in the sentence, for the meaning is: either not [worship Him], so let them worship Him for their security, that is, the blessings of God upon them are beyond counting. If they do not worship Him for all His blessings, then let them worship Him for this single blessing, which is a manifest blessing." End of quotation.

Al-Zajjaj said, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord, so magnify﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:3], "The *fa'* entered to convey the sense of condition, as if it were said: 'Whatever [may be], do not abandon His magnification.'" End of quotation. This is the same meaning as in *al-Kashshaf*. Both of them remained silent about the source from which the sense of condition arises, and that is because such a construction applies when a prepositional phrase or similar complement of the verb is fronted. Consider the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Me, fear [only] Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:40] in the Sura of al-Baqarah; and among such constructions is His saying: ﴿So let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus 10:58] in the Sura of Yunus; and His saying: ﴿So for that, call [them], and remain steadfast﴾ [al-Shura 42:15] in the Sura of al-Shura. And there is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the man who asked him about jihad: he said to him, "Do you have parents?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then strive in service to them."

It is also permissible to make the *lam* dependent on a verb of wonder (*i'jabu*), omitted, which the *lam* indicates, because the *lam* is very frequently used with a complement after expressions of wonder. One says: "How strange, for you!" and "How strange, for that matter!" Among such uses is the line of Imru' al-Qays: "*fa-ya laka min layl*" ("Oh, what a night it is!"). Since the vocative particle is meant here to express wonder, the *fa'* in the words *fal-ya'budu* will be a consequence of the wonder.

So "and summer" is coordinated with an elided noun, that is, "and the journey of summer," because it is evident that one journey cannot begin in two seasons. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the singular word *rihla* be in the genitive construction with two things, since the meaning is clear and there is no ambiguity. Abu Hayyan said: according to Sibawayh, this is not permitted except in cases of necessity.

*Al-shita'* is the name of a season of the solar year, which is divided into four seasons. The season of winter is eighty-nine days and some minutes, beginning with the sun's entry into the sign of Capricorn (*al-Jady*), and ending with the sun's exit from the sign of Pisces (*al-Hut*). Its signs are three: Capricorn, Aquarius (*al-Dalw*), and Pisces. The season of winter is the period of cold.

*Al-sayf* is the name of a season of the solar year, and it is the time of heat. Its duration is ninety-three days and some hours, beginning with the sun's entry into the sign of Cancer (*al-Saratan*), and ending with the sun's exit from the sign of Virgo (*al-Sunbula*). Its signs are three: Cancer, Leo (*al-Asad*), and Virgo.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik said, "Winter is half the year, and summer is half of it. I have always seen Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman and those with him not removing their turbans until the Pleiades (*al-Thurayya*) rises." (He means the rising of the Pleiades at dawn, and that is the first part of summer.) This is the nineteenth day of Bashans, which is the twenty-fifth day according to the Roman or Persian reckoning. The month of Bashans begins on the twenty-sixth day of the month of Nisan (April), and it is thirty days, ending on the 25th of the month of Iyar (May).

Strictly speaking, the year has four seasons: summer is three months, which is what the people of Iraq and Khurasan call spring (*al-rabi'*). Next comes *al-qayz*, three months, which is the intensity of heat. Next comes *al-kharif* (autumn), three months. Next comes winter, three months. This verse is suitable for both terminologies. These two journeys were journeys of trade and provisioning, which Quraysh prepared in these two seasons of the year: one in winter, to the land of Abyssinia, then to Yemen, reaching with them the land of Himyar; and the other in summer, to Syria, reaching with them the city of Busra in the land of Syria.

The one who established these two journeys for them was Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf. The reason for this was that they were afflicted by destitution. When a household did not have food for its sustenance, the head of the household would carry his dependents to a known place, pitch a tent over them, and they would remain there until they died of hunger. This was called *al-i'tifar* (with an unpointed 'ayn, and with a ra', and it was said with a dal instead of the ra', and with a fa'). It happened that a household from the clan of Banu Makhzum was struck by severe poverty, and they resolved to practice *al-i'tifar*. The news reached Hashim, because one of their sons was a foster-brother (*tirb*) of Asad ibn Hashim. Hashim stood up as a speaker among Quraysh and said: "You have introduced an innovation by which you become few and the Arabs multiply, you become humiliated and the Arabs are honoured. You are the people of the sanctuary of God, and the people are followers of you. And this *i'tifar* is about to come upon you." Then he gathered all the sons of one father into two journeys for trade. Whatever the wealthy man gained, he divided between himself and the poor of his clan, until their poor became like their rich. Concerning this, Matrud al-Khuza'i said:

"O man who changes his saddle-bag,
Would that you had alighted with the family of 'Abd Manaf!
Those who take the covenant from its horizons,
And those who journey for the journey of *al-ilaf*.
And those who mix their rich with their poor,
Until their poor becomes like the sufficient."

The two journeys of the *ilaf* of Quraysh continued until Islam came, and they were still upon that.

The well-known and widely reported view is that the one who instituted the *ilaf* (the covenant of safe passage) was Hashim. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-'Arabi reports from al-Harawi that the holders of the *ilaf* were Hashim and his three brothers: 'Abd Shams, al-Muttalib, and Nawfal. Each of them took a *habl* (a covenant, i.e. a pledge of protection) from one of the kings through whose lands they traded: the King of Syria, the King of Abyssinia, the King of Yemen, and the King of Persia. Hashim took it from the King of Syria, who was the King of the Romans. 'Abd Shams took it from the Negus of Abyssinia, al-Muttalib took it from the King of Yemen, and Nawfal took it from Kisra, King of Persia. They would give a *ju'l* (a fee) to the chiefs of the tribes and the leaders of the clans, which was also called *ilaf*. They gave them a share of the profit, carried goods for them, and drove camels to them alongside their own camels, so as to spare them the burden of travel. In return, they protected Quraysh from enemies. Through this, they secured the whole route to Yemen and to Syria, and they were called *al-mujirun* (the protectors).

Al-Naqqash imagined from this that each of these four had a separate journey, and so he claimed that there were four *rihal* (caravan journeys). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view is rejected." Ibn 'Atiyya is right, for the fact that the parties to the covenant by which the *ilaf* was made were four does not require that the journeys be four, since no one has said that. Perhaps these brothers took turns in accompanying the journeys, because they were well known to the tribes through whose lands the caravan passed. Or perhaps they inherited this role after Hashim's death, so that the caravan was attributed to one of them, just as they attributed the caravan that the Muslims intercepted at Badr to Abu Sufyan, since he was then the leader of the people of the valley in Makkah.

The meaning of the verse is a reminder to Quraysh of God's favour upon them: He made easy for them what was not possible for other Arabs, namely security from the aggression of attackers and the raids of raiders throughout the whole year. He also made easy for them the building of the Ka'bah, the institution of the Hajj, their being the custodians of the Sacred Mosque, and He gave them dignity and reverence in the hearts of all the Arabs, both during the sacred months and at other times.

Among the tribes that did not observe the sacred months, such as Tayyi', Quda'ah, and Khath'am, [the journeys] were also made easy for Quraysh, so that the Arab lands from south to north became accessible to them. People in need took refuge with them and travelled with them, and merchants loaded their wares onto them. Makkah became a central point to which goods were brought from all the Arab lands, and from there they were distributed to those who sought them in the rest of the country. Thus the people of Makkah became rich through trade, since they were not people of cultivation or of herding, for they lived in a valley without cultivation. They used to import their food: from Yemen they brought grains of wheat, barley, sorghum, and raisins, as well as leather, cloth, and Yemeni swords; and from Syria they brought grains, dates, olive oil, raisins, cloth, and the *mashrafiyyah* swords. This was in addition to the sacred months that were granted to them along with most of the Arabs, and the festivals and markets of the Hajj that were established for them, as indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾.

This is the explanation for why the command to worship is tied specifically to the favour of this *ilaf*, although God has many favours upon them. This is because the *ilaf* was a comprehensive cause for the most important of the blessings on which their continued existence depended.

The discussion of the meaning of the *fa'* in His words ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ has already been dealt with above, in all its aspects.

The worship they were commanded to perform is the worship of God alone, without associating partners with Him in worship. This is because associating with God someone who does not deserve worship, alongside Him who alone deserves it, is not worship at all. Alternatively, they were preoccupied with worshipping idols instead of God, so they did not mention God except during the days of the Hajj, in the *talbiyah* (the call of pilgrimage). Even so, some of them added to it, after their saying "Labbayka, la sharika laka" (Here I am, You have no partner), the words "illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malaka" (except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns).

The expression of the Lord ("Rabb") as an annexed noun to ﴿this House﴾, rather than saying "So let them worship God," is because the word "Rabb" implies that He deserves to be worshipped exclusively, without any partner.

The annexation of "Rabb" to ﴿this House﴾ was preferred over saying "Their Lord," in order to allude to the fact that the House is the origin of the favour of the *ilaf*, since He commanded Abraham to build the Sacred House, and it was thus the cause of their elevated status among the Arabs. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for mankind﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 97]. This is an incidental reference (*idmaj*) that honours the Sacred House and its excellence.

The House is already known to those addressed, so it is pointed to, because by that prior familiarity it was as though present in the context of the speech. Moreover, the House, defined in this way with the definite article, became a proper name by dominance over the Ka'bah, and the Lord of the House is God, a fact the Arabs acknowledge.

The description of the Lord is given in the relative form ﴿Who fed them against hunger﴾, because of what it implies as a reason for the command to worship the Lord of the Sacred House, by another cause in addition to the favour of making trade easy for them. This is what made them people of wealth, and these two are the favours of feeding them and securing them. This refers to the way in which the ships of Abyssinia were made to come by sea to Jeddah, carrying food to sell there. Quraysh used to go out to Jeddah with camels and donkeys and buy food, a journey of two nights. The people of Taba'lah and Jurash, in the fertile lands of Yemen, used to bring food to Makkah, so they lived in abundance because of the plentiful food in their own land. Likewise, markets were made to be held around Makkah during the months of the Hajj: the market of Majannah, the market of Dhu al-Majaz, and the market of 'Ukaz. There, provisions came to them and their livelihood became broad. It also refers to the fear of Makkah and its people that God placed in the hearts of the Arabs, so that no one wished to harm them by intimidation. This is the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure town and provide its people with fruits﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 126]. This [provision] did not cease to reach them except when the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated against them with the words: "O God, make [the famine] upon them as the years of Joseph." Then they were struck by famine and drought for seven years, and that was at the beginning of the Hijrah.

The *min* that is attached to *ju'* (hunger) and to *khawf* (fear) has the meaning of substitution (*badaliyyah*), that is: He fed them in place of hunger, and secured them in place of fear. The meaning of substitution is that the condition of their land required that its people be hungry. Thus feeding them is a substitute for the hunger that their land would necessitate. Likewise, their condition of small numbers, their being settled people and not people of war, valour, or armed strength, would require that they be exposed to the raids of the tribes. So God gave them security in the Sanctuary instead of the fear that their paucity would entail. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 67].

The indefiniteness of *ju'* (hunger) and *khawf* (fear) is for specification of kind, not for magnification, since no great hunger or fear had befallen them before. Musawwar ibn Hind said in satire of the Banu Asad:

You claimed that your brothers are Quraysh,
for them is the *ilaf*, and for you there is no *ilaf*.
Those were made secure against hunger and fear,
while the Banu Asad have hungered and feared.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Ma'un

This surah is called "Surat al-Ma'un" in many mushafs (codices of the Qur'an) and books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), because the word *al-ma'un* occurs in it and in no other surah.

In some tafsir works it is called "Surat Ara'ayta" (Surat Have You Seen), and likewise in a mushaf from al-Qayrawan from the fifth century; and also al-Bukhari entitled it so in his Sahih.

Ibn 'Atiyya titled it "Surat Ara'ayta alladhi" (Surat Have You Seen the One Who). Al-Kawashi, in *al-Talkhis*, called it "Surat al-Ma'un, al-Din, and Ara'ayta." In *al-Itqan*, it is said: "It is also called Surat al-Din (The Surah of Religion)." In the marginal notes of al-Khafaji and Sa'di it is called Surat al-Takdhib (The Surah of Denial). Al-Biqa'i in *Nazm al-Durar* called it Surat al-Yatim (The Surah of the Orphan). These are six names.

It is Meccan according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Qurtubi reported from Qatadah that it is Medinan, and this is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. In *al-Itqan* it is said: it is said that three verses were revealed first in Makkah, namely up to His words "the poor" (*al-miskin*), and the rest was revealed in Madinah. That is, on the basis that His words ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [Al-Ma'un: 4] through the end of the surah refer to the hypocrites. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Hibat Allah al-Darir, and it is the most apparent view.

It is counted as the seventeenth in the order of the revelation of the surahs, on the basis that it is Meccan. It was revealed after Surat al-Takathur and before Surat al-Kafirun.

Its verses are counted as six by the majority of counters. Al-Alusi related that those who counted its verses as six were the people of Iraq (i.e., Basra and Kufa). Al-Shaykh 'Ali al-Nuri al-Safaqsi said in *Ghayth al-Naf'*: "Its verses are seven according to the Himsi (i.e., Syrian) count, and six in the rest." This contradicts what al-Alusi said.

Among the purposes of this surah is to express astonishment at the state of those who denied the Resurrection, and to condemn their actions: their aggression against the weak and their contempt for him, their withholding of food from the poor, and their turning away from the foundations of Islam, such as prayer and zakat. This is because it does not occur to them that their conduct may bring upon them the anger and punishment of God.

**﴿For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their accustomed journeys in winter and summer, so let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.﴾**

This is a novel opening, since it begins with a prepositional phrase governed by the preposition *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), and there is nothing close by in the sentence that could be linked to it. This creates suspense about what the prepositional phrase depends on. The suspense is heightened by the length of the sentence, since the phrase is separated from what it governs by five words. Thus *li-ilaf* (for the accustomed security) is connected to the words *fal-ya'budu* (so let them worship).

Placing this prepositional phrase first serves to emphasize it, for it is among the reasons for commanding them to worship God, a worship they had abandoned in favour of idol-worship. The prepositional phrase is connected to the verb *li-ya'budu* (let them worship).

The original arrangement of the sentence would be: "Let Quraysh worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear, for the security of their journeys in winter and summer." When the intended emphasis required placing the object before its governing verb, the fronting produced a meaning that made the phrase a condition for its verb. Therefore the verb was joined with the *fa'* (so), which normally belongs to the apodosis of a conditional sentence. The *fa'* that enters the words *fal-ya'budu* indicates that what precedes it has the force of a condition. In other words, it indicates that the fronting of the object is intended to express special emphasis and strong concern, the concern of one who sets a condition for something, while the rest of the sentence is suspended upon it, awaiting its answer. This is a concise and original style.

In *al-Kashshaf*, it is said: "The *fa'* entered because of the sense of condition in the sentence, for the meaning is: either not [worship Him], so let them worship Him for their security, that is, the blessings of God upon them are beyond counting. If they do not worship Him for all His blessings, then let them worship Him for this single blessing, which is a manifest blessing." End of quotation.

Al-Zajjaj said, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord, so magnify﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:3], "The *fa'* entered to convey the sense of condition, as if it were said: 'Whatever [may be], do not abandon His magnification.'" End of quotation. This is the same meaning as in *al-Kashshaf*. Both of them remained silent about the source from which the sense of condition arises, and that is because such a construction applies when a prepositional phrase or similar complement of the verb is fronted. Consider the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Me, fear [only] Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:40] in the Sura of al-Baqarah; and among such constructions is His saying: ﴿So let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus 10:58] in the Sura of Yunus; and His saying: ﴿So for that, call [them], and remain steadfast﴾ [al-Shura 42:15] in the Sura of al-Shura. And there is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the man who asked him about jihad: he said to him, "Do you have parents?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then strive in service to them."

It is also permissible to make the *lam* dependent on a verb of wonder (*i'jabu*), omitted, which the *lam* indicates, because the *lam* is very frequently used with a complement after expressions of wonder. One says: "How strange, for you!" and "How strange, for that matter!" Among such uses is the line of Imru' al-Qays: "*fa-ya laka min layl*" ("Oh, what a night it is!"). Since the vocative particle is meant here to express wonder, the *fa'* in the words *fal-ya'budu* will be a consequence of the wonder.

Al-Farra' and Ibn Ishaq in *al-Sira* permitted that ﴿for the security of Quraysh﴾ be connected to what is in the Sura of al-Fil, namely His saying: ﴿and He made them like eaten straw﴾ [al-Fil 105:5]. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid and the narration of Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. They mean that although this Sura is an independent Sura, it is attached to the Sura of al-Fil. Just as a verse is attached to a verse revealed before it, so too are passages that form a Sura attached to, and dependent upon, a Sura revealed before it.

The original is *alifa*, and the *if'al* form in it is for intensification, because its original function is to indicate that an action occurs from both sides. It came to be used to convey the verbal sense of the act metaphorically, and then this usage spread to some verbs until it equaled the literal sense, as in *safara* (to travel), *'afahu Allah* (God granted him well-being), and *qatalahumu Allah* (God fought them).

It is the name of a kind of fish, strong, which attacks fish and ships.

The two journeys of the *ilaf* of Quraysh continued until Islam came, and they were still upon that.

The commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 106, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2)

The well-known and widely reported view is that the one who instituted the *ilaf* (the covenant of safe passage) was Hashim. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-'Arabi reports from al-Harawi that the holders of the *ilaf* were Hashim and his three brothers: 'Abd Shams, al-Muttalib, and Nawfal. Each of them took a *habl* (a covenant, i.e. a pledge of protection) from one of the kings through whose lands they traded: the King of Syria, the King of Abyssinia, the King of Yemen, and the King of Persia. Hashim took it from the King of Syria, who was the King of the Romans. 'Abd Shams took it from the Negus of Abyssinia, al-Muttalib took it from the King of Yemen, and Nawfal took it from Kisra, King of Persia. They would give a *ju'l* (a fee) to the chiefs of the tribes and the leaders of the clans, which was also called *ilaf*. They gave them a share of the profit, carried goods for them, and drove camels to them alongside their own camels, so as to spare them the burden of travel. In return, they protected Quraysh from enemies. Through this, they secured the whole route to Yemen and to Syria, and they were called *al-mujirun* (the protectors).

Al-Naqqash imagined from this that each of these four had a separate journey, and so he claimed that there were four *rihal* (caravan journeys). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view is rejected." Ibn 'Atiyya is right, for the fact that the parties to the covenant by which the *ilaf* was made were four does not require that the journeys be four, since no one has said that. Perhaps these brothers took turns in accompanying the journeys, because they were well known to the tribes through whose lands the caravan passed. Or perhaps they inherited this role after Hashim's death, so that the caravan was attributed to one of them, just as they attributed the caravan that the Muslims intercepted at Badr to Abu Sufyan, since he was then the leader of the people of the valley in Makkah.

The meaning of the verse is a reminder to Quraysh of God's favour upon them: He made easy for them what was not possible for other Arabs, namely security from the aggression of attackers and the raids of raiders throughout the whole year. He also made easy for them the building of the Ka'bah, the institution of the Hajj, their being the custodians of the Sacred Mosque, and He gave them dignity and reverence in the hearts of all the Arabs, both during the sacred months and at other times.

Among the tribes that did not observe the sacred months, such as Tayyi', Quda'ah, and Khath'am, [the journeys] were also made easy for Quraysh, so that the Arab lands from south to north became accessible to them. People in need took refuge with them and travelled with them, and merchants loaded their wares onto them. Makkah became a central point to which goods were brought from all the Arab lands, and from there they were distributed to those who sought them in the rest of the country. Thus the people of Makkah became rich through trade, since they were not people of cultivation or of herding, for they lived in a valley without cultivation. They used to import their food: from Yemen they brought grains of wheat, barley, sorghum, and raisins, as well as leather, cloth, and Yemeni swords; and from Syria they brought grains, dates, olive oil, raisins, cloth, and the *mashrafiyyah* swords. This was in addition to the sacred months that were granted to them along with most of the Arabs, and the festivals and markets of the Hajj that were established for them, as indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾.

This is the explanation for why the command to worship is tied specifically to the favour of this *ilaf*, although God has many favours upon them. This is because the *ilaf* was a comprehensive cause for the most important of the blessings on which their continued existence depended.

The discussion of the meaning of the *fa'* in His words ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ has already been dealt with above, in all its aspects.

The worship they were commanded to perform is the worship of God alone, without associating partners with Him in worship. This is because associating with God someone who does not deserve worship, alongside Him who alone deserves it, is not worship at all. Alternatively, they were preoccupied with worshipping idols instead of God, so they did not mention God except during the days of the Hajj, in the *talbiyah* (the call of pilgrimage). Even so, some of them added to it, after their saying "Labbayka, la sharika laka" (Here I am, You have no partner), the words "illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malaka" (except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns).

The expression of the Lord ("Rabb") as an annexed noun to ﴿this House﴾, rather than saying "So let them worship God," is because the word "Rabb" implies that He deserves to be worshipped exclusively, without any partner.

The annexation of "Rabb" to ﴿this House﴾ was preferred over saying "Their Lord," in order to allude to the fact that the House is the origin of the favour of the *ilaf*, since He commanded Abraham to build the Sacred House, and it was thus the cause of their elevated status among the Arabs. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for mankind﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 97]. This is an incidental reference (*idmaj*) that honours the Sacred House and its excellence.

The House is already known to those addressed, so it is pointed to, because by that prior familiarity it was as though present in the context of the speech. Moreover, the House, defined in this way with the definite article, became a proper name by dominance over the Ka'bah, and the Lord of the House is God, a fact the Arabs acknowledge.

The description of the Lord is given in the relative form ﴿Who fed them against hunger﴾, because of what it implies as a reason for the command to worship the Lord of the Sacred House, by another cause in addition to the favour of making trade easy for them. This is what made them people of wealth, and these two are the favours of feeding them and securing them. This refers to the way in which the ships of Abyssinia were made to come by sea to Jeddah, carrying food to sell there. Quraysh used to go out to Jeddah with camels and donkeys and buy food, a journey of two nights. The people of Taba'lah and Jurash, in the fertile lands of Yemen, used to bring food to Makkah, so they lived in abundance because of the plentiful food in their own land. Likewise, markets were made to be held around Makkah during the months of the Hajj: the market of Majannah, the market of Dhu al-Majaz, and the market of 'Ukaz. There, provisions came to them and their livelihood became broad. It also refers to the fear of Makkah and its people that God placed in the hearts of the Arabs, so that no one wished to harm them by intimidation. This is the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure town and provide its people with fruits﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 126]. This [provision] did not cease to reach them except when the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated against them with the words: "O God, make [the famine] upon them as the years of Joseph." Then they were struck by famine and drought for seven years, and that was at the beginning of the Hijrah.

The *min* that is attached to *ju'* (hunger) and to *khawf* (fear) has the meaning of substitution (*badaliyyah*), that is: He fed them in place of hunger, and secured them in place of fear. The meaning of substitution is that the condition of their land required that its people be hungry. Thus feeding them is a substitute for the hunger that their land would necessitate. Likewise, their condition of small numbers, their being settled people and not people of war, valour, or armed strength, would require that they be exposed to the raids of the tribes. So God gave them security in the Sanctuary instead of the fear that their paucity would entail. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 67].

The indefiniteness of *ju'* (hunger) and *khawf* (fear) is for specification of kind, not for magnification, since no great hunger or fear had befallen them before. Musawwar ibn Hind said in satire of the Banu Asad:

You claimed that your brothers are Quraysh,
for them is the *ilaf*, and for you there is no *ilaf*.
Those were made secure against hunger and fear,
while the Banu Asad have hungered and feared.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Ma'un

This surah is called "Surat al-Ma'un" in many mushafs (codices of the Qur'an) and books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), because the word *al-ma'un* occurs in it and in no other surah.

In some tafsir works it is called "Surat Ara'ayta" (Surat Have You Seen), and likewise in a mushaf from al-Qayrawan from the fifth century; and also al-Bukhari entitled it so in his Sahih.

Ibn 'Atiyya titled it "Surat Ara'ayta alladhi" (Surat Have You Seen the One Who). Al-Kawashi, in *al-Talkhis*, called it "Surat al-Ma'un, al-Din, and Ara'ayta." In *al-Itqan*, it is said: "It is also called Surat al-Din (The Surah of Religion)." In the marginal notes of al-Khafaji and Sa'di it is called Surat al-Takdhib (The Surah of Denial). Al-Biqa'i in *Nazm al-Durar* called it Surat al-Yatim (The Surah of the Orphan). These are six names.

It is Meccan according to the majority. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Qurtubi reported from Qatadah that it is Medinan, and this is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. In *al-Itqan* it is said: it is said that three verses were revealed first in Makkah, namely up to His words "the poor" (*al-miskin*), and the rest was revealed in Madinah. That is, on the basis that His words ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [Al-Ma'un: 4] through the end of the surah refer to the hypocrites. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Hibat Allah al-Darir, and it is the most apparent view.

It is counted as the seventeenth in the order of the revelation of the surahs, on the basis that it is Meccan. It was revealed after Surat al-Takathur and before Surat al-Kafirun.

Its verses are counted as six by the majority of counters. Al-Alusi related that those who counted its verses as six were the people of Iraq (i.e., Basra and Kufa). Al-Shaykh 'Ali al-Nuri al-Safaqsi said in *Ghayth al-Naf'*: "Its verses are seven according to the Himsi (i.e., Syrian) count, and six in the rest." This contradicts what al-Alusi said.

Among the purposes of this surah is to express astonishment at the state of those who denied the Resurrection, and to condemn their actions: their aggression against the weak and their contempt for him, their withholding of food from the poor, and their turning away from the foundations of Islam, such as prayer and zakat. This is because it does not occur to them that their conduct may bring upon them the anger and punishment of God.
